notes: Considered the first practical, automobile and the first to be put into series production
Considered the first modern car, and a significant advancement over the previous generation of modified stagecoach automobiles.
This 21.5 litre, 'bird-beaked' vehicle set a land speed record of 141 mph, said to be "faster than any plane, train, or automobile" at the time.
The first true 'Bugatti', built in German Alsace before the region became part of France. The car pioneered multivalve engines and was a racing success.
Widely regarded as Britain’s first purpose-built sports car, designed for high-speed endurance trials.
Transformed global manufacturing with the introduction of the world’s first moving assembly line for mass automotive production. Over almost 20 years, Ford produced some 15 million models.
Named 'The Silver Ghost' by virtue of its appearance and "extraordinary stealthiness", Autocar magazine called this "The Best Car in the World" in 1907
The Rumpler Tropfenwagen ("Rumpler drop car", named after its raindrop shape) was developed to be streamlined with a very low drag coefficient.
Britain's answer to the Ford Model T, an economic, mass-produced car, licensed and adapted across Europe, the US and Japan.
World’s first production car to feature a load-bearing monocoque chassis and independent front suspension.
A phenomenally successful racing car, winning over 1,000 races and pioneering the concept of a holistically conceived, race-ready car available for purchase
The first Chrysler car, technically advanced and an affordable price point.
Successfully replaced the Model T by introducing modern driver controls, standard safety glass, and contemporary styling.
Iconic endurance sports car that defined British racing pedigree.
Designed by Ferdinand Porsche, this supercharged performance car dominated hillclimbs and Grand Prix events worldwide.
The pinnacle of pre-war American luxury and power, featuring a DOHC 32-valve straight-eight engine capable of 116 mph.
The outrageous remodelling of the already luxury Cadillac V-16, ordered by by Philippe Barraud, a wealthy playboy of the 1930s, who wanted a bespoke automobile to suit his lavish lifestyle.
Dominant pre-war sports racer featuring a supercharged straight-eight engine and four consecutive Le Mans victories.
Translating literally to 'Front-wheel drive', the Traction Avant pioneered the mass-production front-wheel drive cars.
One of the first cars designed with aerodynamics in mind, in order to reduce airflow
World’s first production car equipped with an electrically powered retractable hardtop roof.
Topolino is Italian for 'little mouse', and this was one of the smallest cars in the world at the time of its production
The pinnacle of pre-war German luxury grand touring, featuring a supercharged straight-eight engine and bespoke coachwork.
Commissioned by Adolf Hitler as an affordable "people's car", this became one of the most produced vehicles in history.
Standardised light four-wheel-drive military vehicle that established the blueprint for all modern off-road vehicles.
Introduced the legendary XK twin-cam engine and debuted as the fastest production car in the world.

Inspired by the US Willys Jeep, thie Land Rover defined British civilian four-wheel-drive capability for decades, with Land Rover claiming in 1992 that 70% of all the vehicles they had built were still in use.
Alec Issigonis-designed family car that democratised post-war British motoring and became the first British vehicle to exceed one million sales.
The first production model to bear the Porsche name, establishing the brand's lightweight, rear-engine sports car identity.

An upscale alternative to the Standard Ford model. It was transformed into "Greased Lightnin'" in the movie Grease, given by Mr Miyagi to Daniel in the Karate Kid, and was Biff Tannen's manure-filled car in Back to the Future
Oldsmobile's most popular line from 1950 to 1974, pairing a lightweight body with the high-compression Rocket V8 engine, establishing the blueprint for the American muscle car.
Saab's first production car. The iconic Saab green was due to Saab aquiring large quantities of a green cellulose paint that was sold off by the armed forces having proved unsuitable for camouflage.
The Lincoln Future concept car was displayed on the auto show circuit in 1955, before being customised by George Barris in 1966 for the TV show, Batman.
First produced in 1963, the DB5 became widely known after being used by James Bond in the 1964 film Goldfinger (although author Ian Fleming had placed Bond in a DB Mark III in the novel).
Herbie, the Love Bug is a fictional sentient 1963 Volkswagen Beetle racing car that was featured in several Walt Disney motion pictures starting with The Love Bug in 1968
The iconic two-door, four-seat small car produced for four decades over a single generation, with over 5 million models made and countless variant and customisations.
The original Mini Cooper S dominated the 1960s rally scene with its light weight and corner-carving ability.

The 1968 Ford Mustang GT Fastback is one of cinema's most famous cars. It is celebrated for starring in a nearly 10-minute, dialogue-free car chase through the streets of San Francisco as Lieutenant Frank Bullitt pursues hitmen in a Dodge Charger
Defined 1970s television cop culture with its distinctive "striped tomato" paint scheme in Starsky & Hutch.
Known as the 'Wet Nellie' and famous for its transformation into a fully functional submarine in the 1977James Bond film, The Spy Who Loved Me.
The iconic car in which Bo "Bandit" Darville gives Sheriff Buford T. Justice the runaround in the 1977 film, Smokey and the Bandit (1977)
The iconic KITT - an artificially intelligent electronic computer module in the body of a highly advanced robotic automobile, that appeared in the TV series Knight Rider.
Converted end-loading ambulance/hearse modified into the gadget-laden, siren-wailing 'Ectomobile' for the 1984 film, Ghostbusters.
Elevated an obscure, commercially failed sports car into an enduring global pop-culture legend via Back to the Future.
Immortalised as the ultimate symbol of automotive desire and teenage rebellion in Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.
The iconic 'A-Team' van, driven by B. A. Baracus
Del Boy's beaten up three-wheel van in the British sitcom, Only Fools and Horses

The iconic orange 1969 Dodge Charger driven in the television series The Dukes of Hazzard. It is known for its signature horn, long jumps, and for having its doors welded shut, requiring the Dukes to climb in and out through the windows.
The iconinc Blues Brothers' Bluesmobile; a decommissioned Mount Prospect police car, purchased by Elwood Blues at an auction after he had traded a previous car for a microphone.
The 308 was made famous by the television series Magnum, P.I. in which the series' lead, Thomas Magnum drove the car around Oahu while on his investigations, from 1980 to 1988
The iconic white Ferrari driven by James "Sonny" Crockett and Ricardo "Rico" Tubbs, two Metro-Dade Police Department detectives working undercover in Miami, Florida.

The 1976 'Mirthmobile' driven by Wayne Campbell and Garth Algar in the 1990s films Wayne's World I and II. The car featured prominently in the films, most notably during the headbanging sing-along to Queen's 'Bohemian Rhapsody'.
The iconic black Lamborghini driven by racer J.J. McClure and his buddy, Victor Prinzim (aka 'Captain Chaos') in the 1981 film, The Cannonball Run
The iconic muscle car used by 'Mad' Max Rockatansky to exact his revenge on an outlaw motorcycle gang who killed his wife and son in the 1979 film, Mad Max
Lightweight John Tojeiro-designed sports car featuring all-independent suspension, forming the engineering base for the Cobra.
Iconic hybrid created by mating a small-block Ford V8 to the lightweight Ace chassis, dominating 1960s sports car racing.
Combined elegant Pietro Frua Italian coachwork with a 7.0-litre Ford V8 built upon an extended Cobra Mk III chassis.
The first vehicle produced by A.L.F.A., featuring advanced multi-valve head engineering and immediate racing success.
Vittorio Jano-designed sports racer that dominated pre-war sports car racing, including multiple Mille Miglia victories.
Pinnacle of pre-war grand touring engineering, combining a twin-supercharged straight-eight engine with advanced independent suspension.
Dominant Grand Prix car that secured victory in the inaugural Formula 1 World Championship race and back-to-back world titles.
Alfa Romeo’s first left-hand-drive car and first unitary chassis, marking the company's transition to mass assembly line manufacturing.
Lightweight compact sports car family that democratised race-derived twin-cam engine performance for mass motoring.
Lightweight, aluminium-panelled homologation special that achieved dominant success in touring car racing worldwide.
Iconic Pininfarina-designed roadster that remained in production across four distinct generations over nearly three decades.
Ultra-exclusive road-going derivative of the Tipo 33 racer featuring butterfly doors and an ultra-high-revving mid-mounted V8.
Groundbreaking front-wheel-drive compact hatchback praised for its boxer engine layout and exceptional dynamic handling.
Avant-garde Zagato-styled sports coupe engineered with race-derived suspension capable of extreme cornering forces.
European Car of the Year winner that revitalised the brand and introduced common-rail direct-injection diesel engines to production cars.
The definitive Alpine model, spanning two distinct eras: the legendary 1960s/70s rally champion and the highly acclaimed modern mid-engined sports car revived in 2017

The Renault Alpine GTA (Gran Tourisme Alpine) is a lightweight, rear-engined sports coupé, designed as a sleek, aerodynamic alternative to contemporary sports cars like the Porsche 944 and Porsche 911
The legendary Audi Quattro introduced four-wheel drive and revolutionized rallying forever.
Key machinery behind Citroën's era of total WRC dominance, securing the first seven of Sébastien Loeb's driver titles.
Three-time WRC Manufacturers' Champion that proved a family saloon could be turned into a rally giant-killer.
One of the most successful rally cars of all time. The Ford works team was practically unbeatable in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
The road-legal RS200 was the basis for Ford's Group B rally car and was designed to comply with FIA homologation regulations, which required 200 cars to be completed
The world's first purpose-built rally supercar, winning three consecutive WRC manufacturers' titles in 1974, 1975 and 1976 in the hands of Sandro Munari and Björn Waldegård
Group A icon that achieved an unprecedented six consecutive WRC Manufacturers' Championships.
Pioneered twincharging by integrating both a supercharger and a turbocharger to deliver instantaneous power.

The Porsche 911 SC RS is one of the most extreme factory rally cars ever built by Porsche. Developed for the FIA's fierce Group B category, the SC RS was an ultra-lightweight, rear-wheel-drive weapon, that dominate tarmac rallies, unlike the complex, all-wheel-drive monsters from rival manufacturers.

One of the most famous endurance rally cars ever constructed. Delays getting the car ready for Group B racing meant Porsche pivoted to the grueling sands of Africa, dominating the 1986 Paris-Dakar Rally with a legendary 1-2 finish

The Peugeot Talbot Sport 205 T16 was the most successful car to compete in the last two years of the World Rally Championship's Group B era, winning the 1985 and 1986 Constructors' and Drivers' titles with Timo Salonen and Juha Kankkunen respectively.
Eschewed turbocharging in favour of a bespoke, naturally aspirated 3.0-litre V6 engine mated to four-wheel drive.
Highly developed Group A special that carried Tommi Mäkinen to four consecutive Drivers' Championships from 1996 to 1999.

Developed in collaboration with performance specialists Cosworth and Irmscher, it was the last highly competitive rear-wheel-drive car built for Group B before turbocharged, all-wheel-drive giants completely took over the World Rally Championship
The ultimate tarmac-focused iteration of the mid-engined 5 Turbo, extracting massive power from a 1.5-litre engine.
Iconic all-wheel-drive performer that defined 1990s WRC culture and propelled Colin McRae to his 1995 world title.
The iconic Toyota rally car of the mid-1990s, most famously associated with WRC champion, Carlos Sainz
Defined the 1.6-litre turbo era by winning four consecutive driver and manufacturer championship doubles.
The car that launched Juan Manuel Fangio onto the Formula 1 stage, winning his very first World Championship in 1951 driving the evolution 159 variant.

Widely considered the most beautiful and perfectly balanced Grand Prix car ever made, the 250F is forever tied to the 1957 German Grand Prix at the Nürburgring, in which Juan Manuel Fangio recovered from a botched pit-stop by breaking the track lap record ten times in a row, winning the race on the final lap and securing the F1 title.
Built and  tailored specifically for Juan Manual Fangio, he used it to dominate and capture back-to-back F1 World Championships in 1954 and 1955
Lotus revolutionised F1 by making lighter, tighter, sleeker cars. Jim Clark weaponised the Lotus 25, taking 14 Grand Prix victories and capturing the 1963 F1 World Championship in dominant fashion

The Lotus 49 pioneered two massive structural design milestones: the fully integrated stressed-member engine and the dawn of aerodynamic wings. It won on its debut in 1967 with Jim Clark, carried Graham Hill to the 1968 title, and secured Lotus the 1968 and 1970 Constructors' Championships
The Lotus 72 looked like a spaceship compared to anything else on the grid, establishing the visual silhouette that modern Formula 1 cars still use today.

The iconic black and gold livery on the Lotus 79, a car which introduced 'Ground Effect' aerodynamics that created a vacuum literally sucking the car onto the track. The Lotus 79 was so vastly superior to the rest of the field in 1978 that Mario Andretti easily cruised to the World Championship, securing Lotus its final Constructors' title.

One of the most successful and dominant Formula One car designs of all time. The MP4/4 gave Ayrton Senna his first F1 World Championship in 1988 and laid the foundation for a fierce competition between Senna and teammate Alain Prost over the following years.

The Williams FW14B is arguably the most technologically advanced Formula 1 car ever built relative to its competition, dominating the 1992 season, and giving Nigel Mansell his only F1 World Championship in 1992

The F2004 is widely recognized as Michael Schumacher's best and most dominant Formula 1 car, representing the peak of the Schumacher, Ross Brawn, and Jean Todt "Dream Team" era. During the 2004 season, it proved to be practically untouchable, securing Schumacher his seventh and final World Championship

Representing the peak of the ultra-high-downforce turbo-hybrid era, the W11 was famously described by Lewis Hamilton as "the best F1 car the team has ever produced", and propelled him to his record-equalling seventh World Championship
Statistically the most dominant F1 car ever built, winning 21 out of 22 Grand Prix races in a single season.
Australia’s first mass-produced car, establishing the domestic automotive manufacturing industry.
Unique Australian-designed fibreglass micro-sports car built on an imported German chassis, made famous in a 1990s Yellow Pages TV advert.
The Holden Monaro GTS 327 was Holden's first sports coupe, won the brand's first Bathurst 500 victory, and ignited the legendary "Ford vs. Holden" racetrack war.

Celebrated as Australia’s greatest premier home-grown V8 sports car, pairing a lightweight fibreglass body with Ford V8 power. Unlike the mainstream heavy-iron muscle cars from Ford and Holden, the Nagari was a sleek, lightweight fiberglass boutique sports car designed to take on European marques like Lotus and TVR.
Peak of early Australian muscle, famously claiming the title of the world’s fastest production four-door sedan upon release.
Iconic short-wheelbase muscle car featuring a potent 265 cu in "Hemi" straight-six with triple Weber carburettors.
The best-selling generation of this ubiquitous car of Australian automotive history, family life and motorsport, which lasted for 40 years across four generations.
Rugged executive saloon built to withstand harsh climate conditions, serving as the primary Soviet official and taxi vehicle.
Distinctive aerodynamic rear-engined V8 luxury car reserved exclusively for high-ranking party officials and foreign dignitaries.
Duroplast-bodied "people's car" that became an enduring cultural icon of East German motoring.
Skoda's economic alternative to the western rear-engined family cars like the Renault 8 or VW Beetle.
License-built modification of the Fiat 124/125 that formed the backbone of Polish post-war passenger transport.
License-built variant of the Renault 12 that served as Romania’s primary national family car for over three decades.
The Lada Niva has been in continuous production since 1977 and pioneered the modern compact crossover layout by offering permanent four-wheel drive to rural, urban and family users.
Hatchback family car engineered with over one million units produced and remaining a Polish staple for decades.
The Yugo was derived from the Fiat 127 and became Yugoslavia's most famous international automotive export.
Bertone-styled front-wheel-drive hatchback that modernized the brand and paved the way for its Volkswagen acquisition.
The compact / supermini car launched by Renault's Romanian division, Dacia, and immortalised in a long-running joke on the TV series, Top Gear
All-electric hypercar that set global acceleration records and redefined electric vehicle performance limits.
Unibody compact saloon featuring a safety cage design that established Volvo's global export footprint.
Iconic family car that became the first vehicle in the world to feature three-point seatbelts as standard equipment.
Aerodynamic, rally-winning compact car that established Saab’s international reputation for durability and engineering.
Sleek sports coupe famous for its TV appearance in The Saint and for setting the highest certified vehicle mileage record.
Defining boxy Swedish estate and saloon that served as the international benchmark for passenger crash safety for decades.
Massively influential sports saloon that democratised forced-induction turbocharging technology for everyday family cars.
Iconic executive car featuring aircraft-inspired ergonomics, a wrapped windscreen, and distinctive turbo performance.
Shattered performance estate stereotypes with a high-output turbocharged five-cylinder engine and BTCC racing lineage.
Inaugural production hypercar from Christian von Koenigsegg, introducing dihedral synchro-helix doors and record-breaking engineering.
Benchmark luxury family SUV that pioneered advanced rollover protection systems and versatile seven-seat packaging.
Early Scandinavian pioneer of plastic-bodied, purpose-built urban electric vehicles.
Land-speed record holder that cemented Sweden at the pinnacle of hypercar performance with a 277 mph top speed.
High-volume all-electric fastback that launched Volvo's standalone performance EV brand into global markets.
Based on the Morris Oxford III, this iconic "King of Indian Roads" served politicians and public transport fleets for over five decades.
Licence-built derivative of the Fiat 1100 Delight that became the quintessential Mumbai taxi and a symbol of mid-century urban transport.
Suzuki-derived compact hatchback that democratised personal car ownership and transformed India's automotive landscape.
Rugged, lightweight off-roader based on the Suzuki SJ410 that became a mainstay for the Indian Armed Forces and local rally sport.
Pioneering sports utility vehicle that launched as India's first indigenously designed passenger SUV with signature rear alpine glass.
Purpose-built multi-utility vehicle designed completely in-house, establishing market dominance across rural and commercial transport.
India's first fully home-grown passenger car, offering unprecedented interior space and launching Tata as a high-volume passenger brand.
Clean-sheet global SUV platform that successfully transitioned Mahindra from a tractor/utility maker into a modern SUV manufacturer.
Engineered as the world's most affordable production car to provide safer, weather-protected transport for families upgrading from motorcycles.
Rugged off-roader rooted in early Jeep CJ assembly legacy that evolved into India’s primary mainstream lifestyle 4x4.
Developed and built in limited numbers as India's first indigenous mid-engined sports car.
China’s first official state limousine, built specifically for government ceremonies and high-ranking political leadership.
Served as the primary government official and taxi fleet passenger car across China for nearly three decades.
Ubiquitous microvan that mobilised small businesses across China, becoming one of the highest-selling vehicle platforms globally.
Ultra-affordable supermini that democratised private car ownership for millions of first-time Chinese buyers.
Groundbreaking saloon that debuted as the world's first mass-produced plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV).
Compact MPV that dominated domestic sales charts for a decade as China's ultimate multipurpose family and commercial workhorse.
Electric supercar that set lap records at the Nürburgring, establishing China's capacity for high-performance EV engineering.
Landmark SUV that showcased the rapid rise of Chinese domestic brands in design sophistication, safety, and technology integration.
Ultra-compact EV that spearheaded mass urban electrification through extreme affordability and minimalist packaging.
Globally distributed electric crossover that marked the forefront of China's transformation into a major international vehicle exporter.
High-tech luxury off-roader featuring independent quad-motor torque vectoring and emergency water-floating capability.
High-profile electric performance saloon that demonstrated the rapid entry of consumer tech giants into mainstream automotive manufacturing.
Argentina's first indigenous series-produced automobile, designed and built by Horacio Anasagasti.
Rugged utility estate designed and manufactured specifically to meet the demands of rural South America.
Licence-built derivative of the BMC Farina saloon that became the quintessential mid-century Argentine taxi icon.
Advanced hand-built sports coupe featuring a hand-hammered steel body, serving as one of Brazil's earliest GT cars.
Celebrated Argentine performance icon that adapted American underpinnings with Pininfarina styling and local engine engineering.
Iconic fibreglass-bodied sports car export that became Brazil's most famous independent automotive manufacturer.
Striking sports coupe designed entirely in Brazil to circumvent strict national restrictions on foreign imports.
Indigenously designed Brazilian hatchback-estate hybrid that achieved massive commercial success across Latin America.
Adapted Fiat 127 derivative that pioneered the world’s first mass-produced ethanol-fuelled production engine in 1979.
Unique Mexican hatchback-saloon hybrid developed locally by Vehículos Automotores Mexicanos using AMC components.
Microcar engineered as the first fully indigenous, 100% Brazilian-designed and manufactured city vehicle.
Mexico's first internally designed and built lightweight sports car, constructed with an aluminium spaceframe.
Ultra-lightweight track-focused supercar engineered in Mexico for high-performance international exports.
Recognized as South Africa’s first commercially built production car, featuring a fibreglass body on a tubular frame.
Lightweight fibreglass sports car developed by Glass Sport Motors that achieved notable racing success in Europe and Africa.
Egypt’s first state-backed national automobile project, based on NSU Prinz underpinnings.
V8-powered homologation special created in South Africa that dominated local saloon car racing with factory approval from Ford.
Unique South African continuation of the Mk1 Golf platform that remained a dominant sales success for 25 years.
Rare, South Africa-exclusive E30 developed with Alpina, cramming a 3.2-litre 6-cylinder engine into a compact chassis.
Bespoke South African Group N homologation special featuring aluminium body panels, evolving into a major national cultural icon.
Morocco's first supercar, featuring a quad-turbocharged V12 engine and carbon-fibre construction.
Minimalist fibreglass utility vehicle that established Tunisia's modern indigenous motor manufacturing presence.
Developed at Makerere University, serving as Africa’s first locally engineered electric vehicle prototype.
Stripped-back, durable SUV purpose-built in Kenya to handle rough terrain and heavy loads at a low cost point.
Launched as part of Nigeria's first fully indigenous vehicle manufacturing and mass-assembly enterprise.
The longest continuous vehicle nameplate in history, evolving across 12 generations from a truck-based station wagon into a full-size SUV.
The original air-engined design achieved 65 years of unbroken continuous production across global factories before the final classic car rolled off the line in Mexico.
Continuous production through 14 generations, establishing itself as one of the world's most commercially successful pickup truck lines.
Unbroken manufacturing run spanning seven generations, evolving from the original air-cooled T1 split-screen to modern passenger and commercial variants.
Originating as the BJ light 4x4, it is Toyota's longest continuously produced vehicle line, famous for heavy-duty off-road durability.
America's longest unbroken sports car production run, spanning eight generations and transitioning from a front- to mid-engine layout.
Continuous production of luxury grand tourers and roadsters across seven generations, tracing directly back to the 300 SL.
Continuous production run starting under Prince Motor Company, evolving through 13 generations from compact saloon to modern sports sedan.
Achieved a 41-year unbroken production run for the original single-generation Alec Issigonis design before manufacturing ceased in 2000.
Unbroken 60-plus year production run of the iconic rear-engined sports car, evolving through eight distinct mechanical generations.
Continuous production across seven generations, pioneering the pony car segment and remaining in uninterrupted manufacture.
The world's top-selling nameplate, maintaining unbroken global production through 12 generations since its 1966 introduction.
Continuous global production across 11 generations, transforming from a basic subcompact into a premier global family hatchback and saloon.
Uninterrupted production run spanning eight generations, defining the modern European front-wheel-drive hatchback segment.
Continuous production through seven generations as the global benchmark for executive sports saloons.
Pioneered the Mediterranean "Spiaggina" style beach car, complete with wicker seats, doorless sides, and a cloth awning canopy.
Originally engineered as a lightweight military vehicle, it evolved into a classic open-air resort cruiser.
The original glass-fibre dune buggy built on a shortened VW Beetle floorpan, sparking a global kit-car phenomenon.
Minimalist, doorless utility beach vehicle built by Carrozzeria Savio using standard Fiat 600 running gear.
Open-top civilian leisure adaptation derived from East Germany's military Kübelwagen version of the 601.
Australian-designed, Beetle-based open utility and beach vehicle built to handle rugged local conditions.
Lightweight utility and leisure car with a corrugated ABS plastic body based on the 2CV chassis.
Doorless, open-top beach car conversion of the Renault 4 saloon built in limited numbers.
Utilitarian military and civilian recreation vehicle featuring flat metal panels, detachable doors, and a fold-down windscreen.
Glass-fibre open leisure vehicle range designed on various Renault platforms to compete directly with the Méhari.
Open-top plastic and steel body beach/leisure vehicles built by Italian coachbuilder Moretti using Fiat Panda underpinnings.
The company's inaugural single-cylinder vehicle that earned the 1908 Dewar Trophy for standardized interchangeable parts.
Landmark early vehicle whose derivative introduced the world's first production electric self-starter and lighting in 1912.
Pioneered the first mass-produced V8 engine in a passenger vehicle, establishing the brand's mechanical reputation.
Ultra-exclusive pre-war flagship powered by the world's first commercially produced V16 engine.
Designed by Bill Mitchell, it established the modern notchback three-box saloon silhouette with an integrated boot.
The 1959, 6th generation Cadillac 62 is remembered for its iconic huge tailfins with dual bullet tail lights.
Hand-built halo car featuring a stainless steel roof, self-levelling air suspension, and memory seats.
Showcased the absolute peak of 1950s tailfin design before evolving into Cadillac's core luxury saloon line.
Radical front-wheel-drive personal luxury coupe featuring sharp, razor-edge styling and hidden headlamps.
Introduced as an "internationally sized" compact luxury saloon built to counter high-end European imports.
Pininfarina-styled roadster assembled using an extraordinary 3,300-mile air-freight supply line between Italy and Detroit.
Full-size luxury SUV that revitalised the brand's commercial status and became a major cultural icon.
High-performance sports saloon developed on the Nürburgring to directly challenge established European performance divisions.
Purpose-built crossover marking the start of Cadillac's transition to a fully electric model lineup.
World's first mass-produced assembly-line automobile, establishing Ransom E. Olds as an early automotive pioneer.
Giant pre-war luxury vehicle featuring 42-inch wheels, representing the height of early American Brass Era opulence.
Introduced GM's "Hydra-Matic" transmission for the 1940 model year, creating the world's first fully automatic mass-market gearbox.
The division's flagship luxury saloon line, showcasing top-tier GM comfort and technological features across ten generations.
Groundbreaking compact performance coupe that was among the very first passenger cars equipped with a turbocharged engine.
Muscle car icon, named for its original setup of a 4-barrel carburettor, 4-speed manual gearbox, and dual exhausts.
Landmark front-wheel-drive personal luxury coupe featuring radical styling and a unitised transaxle layout.
Limited-production muscle car collaboration with Hurst Performance, famous for its distinctive paint schemes and "Lightning Rod" shifters.
Full-size family estate wagon famous for its 1970s power "Clamshell" tailgate that glided into the floor structure.
Massively popular mid-size series that became the single best-selling car model in North America during the late 1970s and 1980s.
Experimental quad-cam land-speed research vehicle that set multiple closed-course world records driven by A.J. Foyt.
Sleek, rigid sports saloon powered by a Northstar-derived V8, created in an effort to modernise and revitalise the brand.
Credited with popularising the 1960s American muscle car trend by fitting a 389 cu in V8 into a mid-size chassis.
High-performance derivative of the Mustang fastback equipped with Ford's big-block Cobra Jet V8 engine.
Mid-size GM A-body muscle icon that reached its performance pinnacle with the 450 bhp LS6 454 V8 in 1970.
Coke-bottle styled hardtop coupe famed for its optional 426 Hemi engine and pop culture presence.
Back-to-basics budget muscle car equipped with a spartan interior, Warner Bros. horn sound, and big V8 power.
Named for its 4-barrel carburettor, 4-speed manual gearbox, and dual exhausts, offering refined performance.
Unique steel-bodied two-seater muscle car developed by American Motors as a lighter, shorter Corvette competitor.
Radical aerodynamic NASCAR homologation special fitted with a protruding nose cone and high-mounted rear wing.
High-luxury Gran Sport derivative powered by a massive 455 cu in V8 delivering a legendary 510 lb·ft of torque.
Chrysler’s E-body entry into the muscle car wars, offering a wide array of powertrains up to the 426 Hemi.
1980s turbo V6 legend in all-black trim whose limited-run GNX variant out-accelerated contemporary sports cars.
Drag-strip-optimised factory muscle car producing up to 840 bhp, complete with transbrake and drag radial tyres.
Argentine automotive icon blending American Rambler underpinnings, a high-compression straight-six engine, and Pininfarina styling.
Marketed as Europe’s answer to the Mustang, offering fastback pony car styling paired with Essex V6 powertrains.
Executive German saloon equipped with an imported 5.4-litre Chevrolet V8, combining American muscle torque with European chassis dynamics.
South African homologation special that shoehorned a 5.0-litre Ford Windsor V8 into a Mk1 Capri bodyshell with factory endorsement.
Japanese fastback coupe heavily influenced by American muscle styling, featuring a rear ducktail spoiler and dual-overhead-cam engine options.
Legendary four-door Australian muscle saloon built for Bathurst homologation, powered by a 351 cu in Cleveland V8.
Brazil’s quintessential muscle car, featuring bold rally stripes and a high-torque 4.1-litre inline-six engine based on an Opel platform.
Short-wheelbase Australian muscle coupe powered by a triple-Weber-carburetted 265 cu in "Hemi" straight-six engine.
Wild South African homologation special stuffing a 5.0-litre Z28 Camaro V8 into a lightweight Vauxhall Firenza body.
Widely dubbed "Britain’s first supercar", featuring aggressive muscular styling, a blanked-off grille, and a 375 bhp 5.3-litre V8.
Compact V8 touring car homologation special that achieved legendary motorsport dominance at the Bathurst 1000.
The ultimate swan song for Australian muscle manufacturing, powered by a supercharged 6.2-litre Corvette ZR1 V8 engine.
Iconic two-door sport wagon featuring a distinct grooved roofline and frameless door glass, establishing the American sports estate layout.
Bespoke coachbuilt sports estate created by Harold Radford, originally commissioned by company owner David Brown to carry his polo gear and hunting dogs.
Fibreglass-bodied pioneer that popularised the practical two-door sports estate concept for the mass market.
Sporting estate derivative of the P1800 featuring an all-glass frameless rear hatch, nicknamed "Schneewittchensarg" (Snow White's Coffin) in Germany.
"High Performance Estate" designed in-house, blending a sports coupe front end with a stylish shooting brake tailgate.
Unconventional shooting brake-proportioned sports car engineered for high torsional rigidity, affectionately nicknamed the "Clown Shoe".
Giorgetto Giugiaro-designed sports 2+2 featuring a steep glass tailgate and distinct shooting brake proportions.
Pininfarina-styled, four-seat V12 flagship featuring a four-wheel-drive system and a true two-door shooting brake bodyshell.
Modern four-door luxury interpretation featuring a swept roofline and an optional cherry wood luggage compartment floor.
Ultra-limited coachbuilt V12 grand tourer featuring Zagato’s signature double-bubble roof motif extending into a glass-roofed rear deck.
Tailored specifically for the European market, blending executive saloon chassis tuning with a swept estate silhouette.
